items.alt: A telescope observes a receding source. Aligned spectral scales show a line shifting from 500 to 505 nm, corresponding to z = 0.010.
Aligned spectral lines compare 500 nm at rest with 505 nm observed, a 5 nm redshift.
The fractional wavelength shift is 5 nm divided by 500 nm, giving dimensionless z = 0.010.
The telescope observes a source moving away along the line of sight; the low-speed Doppler estimate is 3,000 km/s.
Two matched spectral lines share z = 0.010: 500 becomes 505 nm and 600 becomes 606 nm.
A receding source shifts a 500 nm line to 505 nm, implying z = 0.010 and an approximate radial speed of 3,000 km/s.
The proton-proton chain builds helium through deuterium and helium-3, releasing positrons, neutrinos, and energy.
Solar fusion supplies energy to hot plasma; neutrinos escape readily while radiation transfers energy through many interactions.
A cutaway Sun distinguishes the radiative zone, where radiation repeatedly interacts, from the convection zone, where moving plasma transports energy.
Light escapes near the photosphere, and cooler gas produces dark absorption lines in the observed spectrum.
Individual detector events are localized; many detections reveal a wave-like probability pattern when two coherent paths contribute.
An upward transition absorbs a photon; a downward transition emits one. Photon energy equals the difference between allowed energy levels.
Matching multiple spectral lines connects a source with a laboratory reference; allowed atomic energy differences produce characteristic patterns.
A longer observed wavelength indicates recession under the Doppler model; the illustrated line shifts from 500 to 505 nm.
Corresponding lines shift by the same fraction: 500 to 505 nm and 600 to 606 nm both give z = 0.010.
Top-view diagram of wavefronts spreading from two slit openings and overlapping to produce bright and dark detector regions.
Individual photon detections appear as localized dots on a dimensional detector screen.
Parent-isotope populations halve statistically while individual decay times remain unpredictable; small samples fluctuate around expected counts.
Localized photon detections accumulate into an interference distribution, linking discrete detection with wave-like probability amplitudes.
Countable shaded spheres show carbon-14 with six protons and eight neutrons, giving atomic number 6 and mass number 14.
Carbon-12 and carbon-14 each contain six protons, but have six and eight neutrons respectively; carbon-12 is stable and carbon-14 is radioactive.
In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton, with an emitted electron and electron antineutrino. Mass number is unchanged and atomic number rises by one.
Alpha decay emits two protons and two neutrons; daughter mass number decreases by four and atomic number by two.
Beta-minus decay transforms a neutron into a proton, emitting an electron and electron antineutrino; A is unchanged and Z increases by one.
Gamma emission releases excitation energy as a photon without changing the proton or neutron counts, so A and Z remain unchanged.
Dimensional comparison of alpha decay, beta-minus decay, and gamma emission, tracking mass number and atomic number.
An alpha particle contains two protons and two neutrons; alpha decay lowers A by four and Z by two.
Beta-minus decay creates a proton, electron, and electron antineutrino from a neutron; nuclear mass number stays constant and atomic number rises by one.
An excited nucleus emits a gamma photon and loses energy while its mass number and atomic number remain unchanged.
An energy ledger shows initial rest-mass energy balanced by product rest-mass energy plus released energy; 0.0200 u corresponds to 18.6 MeV.
Alpha, beta-minus, and gamma diagrams summarize how nuclear changes affect A, Z, and excitation energy.
After one half-life, 50 of an initial 100 parent nuclei are expected to remain; actual small populations fluctuate.
Expected parent counts halve successively from 100 to 50 to 25, while decay products remain in the sample.
Four runs beginning with 20 nuclei leave 12, 8, 11, and 9 parents after one half-life, illustrating fluctuation around the expected count of 10.
Four dimensional sample trays show parent mass halving from 80 to 40 to 20 to 10 mg over 18 hours.
The timeline has three equal six-hour intervals: 0, 6, 12, and 18 hours.
Remaining parent mass halves in sequence: 80 mg, 40 mg, 20 mg, and 10 mg. Gray symbols represent decay products.
Three half-lives reduce the expected parent fraction to one-eighth, leaving 10 mg from 80 mg.
After 18 hours, one-eighth of the parent isotope remains. Decay products remain represented in each sample tray.
Summary: parent mass falls from 80 mg to 10 mg over three six-hour half-lives; individual decay times remain unpredictable.
A neutron is absorbed by uranium-235, forming excited uranium-236 before it divides into fission fragments.
One possible fission produces barium-141, krypton-92, and three neutrons, conserving nucleon number and charge.
A branching chain reaction grows when each fission causes more than one further fission on average; one gives a steady rate.
Neutrons may trigger fission, escape, or be absorbed by control rods. Moderators slow neutrons rather than absorbing them for control.
A steady chain reaction averages one further fission per fission; other neutrons may escape or be absorbed in control rods.
A growing chain reaction has more than one further fission per fission on average, illustrated by branching neutron paths.
Two protons form deuterium, a positron, and an electron neutrino in the first proton-proton chain stage.
Deuterium combines with a proton to form helium-3 and emit a gamma photon. The first two stages occur twice before the next reaction.
Two helium-3 nuclei form helium-4 and return two protons, conserving six nucleons and total charge.
Initial rest-mass energy becomes product rest-mass energy plus released energy, conserving total mass-energy. The numerical example is hypothetical.
Neutron-induced fission splits a heavy uranium nucleus into smaller fragments and releases neutrons and energy.
The proton-proton chain combines light nuclei through deuterium and helium-3 to produce helium-4 and release energy.
Dimensional power-plant cutaway traces fission heat through a separate coolant and steam loop to the turbine, generator, and condenser.
Fission fragments, neutrons, and radiation carry released energy; collisions convert much of it into thermal energy.
A closed primary coolant loop carries heat from the reactor core to a heat exchanger and returns cooler fluid to the reactor.
The heat exchanger transfers energy from primary coolant to a separate secondary steam loop without mixing the fluids.
Steam turns a turbine shaft, then a condenser removes heat so water can return to the heat exchanger.
The turbine shaft drives a generator that supplies electrical energy; some energy leaves as heat to the surroundings.
In top view, coherent incident wavefronts reach a barrier with two openings and a detector beyond it.
Curved wavefronts spread from both slit openings and overlap in the region beyond the barrier.
Overlapping contributions produce alternating bright and dark regions at the detector, illustrating interference.
With two coherent paths and no which-path measurement, isolated photons produce separate localized detector events.
A single photon detection appears as one localized dot; it does not reveal the full probability pattern.
Many localized photon detections accumulate in dense and sparse bands, revealing an interference probability pattern.
A photon must carry enough energy to overcome the metal surface work function before an electron can escape.
Below-threshold photons do not eject electrons in the single-photon model; above threshold the remaining energy can become electron kinetic energy.
At fixed frequency above threshold, greater intensity supplies more photons and can eject more electrons without increasing maximum electron kinetic energy.
Increasing photon frequency increases energy per photon; emission requires enough energy to overcome the surface work function.
Greater intensity at fixed frequency increases photon flux, not energy per photon or maximum emitted-electron kinetic energy.
Metal surfaces illustrate below-threshold and above-threshold photon interactions for a photoelectric comparison.
Each incoming photon carries energy set by its frequency; compare this energy with the work function of the metal.
Above-threshold photon energy can remove an electron from the surface, leaving energy available as kinetic energy.
The maximum emitted-electron kinetic energy equals photon energy hf minus the work function phi.
A photon below the surface threshold cannot eject an electron in the ordinary single-photon model.
The comparison summarizes why above-threshold light can eject electrons while below-threshold light cannot.
A polarizing filter selects an electric-field direction transverse to propagation, producing linearly polarized light.
Parallel polarizer axes transmit light; crossed axes at 90 degrees ideally block transmission.
A receding source shifts spectral lines to longer wavelengths; the example compares 500 nm at rest with 505 nm observed.
Dimensional RGB spotlights illustrate additive color mixing: red and green make yellow, green and blue cyan, red and blue magenta, and all three white.
